name: The Year in Feasts: How Holidays and Festivals Began
description: From harvest rites and midwinter parties to national days and rock festivals: where our holidays came from and how they changed on the way.

checkpoints.name: Rites of the seasons
checkpoints.note: Farming peoples marked the seasons with rites: the Eleusinian Mysteries in Greece, Nowruz in Persia, Chinese New Year and the Roman Saturnalia, while Hanukkah recalled the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem. The Roman calendar tried to keep dates in step with the sun.

checkpoints.name: Faith and the calendar
checkpoints.note: Christmas was set in the Julian calendar and Easter became the main Christian feast. Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha follow the Islamic calendar, and Passover and other Jewish feasts the Hebrew calendar. Diwali, Holi and Vesak mark seasons and faith in South Asia, the Maya kept their own count, and Gion Matsuri and Hanami began in Japan.

checkpoints.name: Feasts and masks
checkpoints.note: The Gregorian calendar fixed the year in 1582. Carnival and the Carnival of Venice let people wear masks before Lent, Halloween grew from older autumn customs, and the Day of the Dead blended Aztec and Christian ideas. Valentine's Day was linked with romance in this age, and the Kumbh Mela and the Mid-Autumn Festival drew crowds in Asia.

checkpoints.name: Nations celebrate
checkpoints.note: Revolutionary France briefly tried its own calendar. Oktoberfest started as a royal wedding party, and Thanksgiving, Bastille Day and Mother's Day became national or family days in the United States and France. Rio's Carnival grew into one of the biggest street festivals.

checkpoints.name: The festival age
checkpoints.note: Edinburgh's Fringe, La Tomatina and Notting Hill Carnival add street parties and stages, and Woodstock, Glastonbury and Burning Man turn music and art into a gathering of tens of thousands.
